adaptive.difficulty_levers: path length, forward vs reverse, pad spacing and density, presentation speed, optional retention delay
adaptive.notes: Paths are procedurally generated and length is a native staircase, giving matched parallel routes.

engagement_hook: Guide a lost firefly home by walking its glowing trail backwards; longer trails feel like braver journeys.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor/device: mis-taps on close pads are mitigated by large, well-spaced targets and tap-not-drag. Attention/ADHD: impulsive tapping inflates errors, so error types are separated and engagement is gated before tail calls. Familiarity: reverse-retrace self-teaches via the ghost-hand and warm-up. Strategy learning: reversing a path can be partly strategic, so path and efficiency are reported alongside pure span.

name: Mobile Stash (nonverbal complex span)
one_liner: The child answers a quick nonverbal puzzle (which side of the beam tips? is it symmetric? which way does the piece point?) then remembers a charm hung on a mobile; after several cycles taps the charms back in order.
interaction: Each cycle shows a processing puzzle answered with a two-choice tap - toggle among BALANCE (which side of the beam tips, or is it level: a nonverbal operation), SYMMETRY (is the hanging pattern mirror-symmetric), ROTATE (which upright direction the tilted charm points) and COUNT (how many charms of a target kind) - then briefly hangs a coloured charm at a position to remember. After N cycles the child taps the charms back in presentation order. Set size rises when recall is perfect AND processing stayed accurate, falls otherwise; processing is time-limited so it cannot be skipped.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps the heavier side of a beam, a charm appears, it does one more cycle, then taps the two charms back in order with a check mark (about 9s); one unscored warm-up follows. Icons (scale, mirror, curved arrow, tally) show the current puzzle with no text.

learning_science.why: Complex span (interleaving processing and storage) predicts fluid intelligence because it taxes attention control, not just storage.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Interleave a nonverbal processing judgment with spatial storage and score the recalled span.
learning_science.source: Engle, R. W. (2002). Working memory capacity as executive attention. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 11(1), 19-23.

learning_science.why: Symmetry and other visuospatial complex spans are reliable, largely language-free capacity measures.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Anchor young and low-literacy bands with the symmetry and balance modules and spatial charm storage.
learning_science.source: Kane, M. J., Hambrick, D. Z., Tuholski, S. W., Wilhelm, O., Payne, T. W., & Engle, R. W. (2004). The generality of working memory capacity. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 133(2), 189-217.

learning_science.why: A storage span is valid only if the child actually performs the processing task rather than trading it away.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Enforce a processing-accuracy gate (at least 80%) before crediting a storage span.
learning_science.source: Conway, A. R. A., Kane, M. J., Bunting, M. F., Hambrick, D. Z., Wilhelm, O., & Engle, R. W. (2005). Working memory span tasks: A methodological review and user's guide. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 12(5), 769-786.

tail_precision_rationale: Interleaving a nonverbal judgment with spatial storage taxes attention control, not storage alone: the adaptive recall span (M-SPAN, M-DIFFREACH) is a continuous above-grade capacity index, position partial-credit (M-POLY) extracts graded tail signal, and processing accuracy (M-PROCACC) gates the storage score so children who neglect the puzzle to inflate recall are flagged; error typing (M-ERRTYPE), cross-form consistency (M-CONSIST) and low processing-task RT variability (M-RTVAR) mark secure high-capacity solvers rather than fast guessers.
age_rationale: Dual-tasking with a secondary judgment overloads most K-1 executive control, so the floor is 2-3 using the simplest balance or symmetry module at set size 2; rotation, counting and larger sets suit 4-5 and 6-8, and the reading module is age-gated to 4-5 and up. Responses are taps only.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 balance/symmetry span at set size 2 up to 6-8 rotation/operation span at set sizes 4-5 with an optional reading module
adaptive.difficulty_levers: set size, processing module and its difficulty/time limit, processing-storage similarity, charm-position density
adaptive.notes: Processing items and charm layouts are generated and set size is a native staircase; the processing-accuracy gate must be enforced for a valid span.

engagement_hook: A hanging-mobile balancing game where you solve a quick puzzle then stash a charm, proving you can juggle thinking and remembering at once.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Academic skill: operation and reading modules confound with math and literacy, so young or low-literacy children use the balance, symmetry and rotation modules and processing accuracy is reported separately. Attention/ADHD: dual-tasking amplifies attention effects, so gate on M-PROCACC and engagement. Speed-accuracy trade-off on processing is caught by M-PROCACC. Colour vision: charms use distinct hues plus shape redundancy. Motor/familiarity: large targets and a warm-up.

name: Recipe Recall (verbal/numeric complex span)
one_liner: Between remembering each ingredient the child answers a quick check (does this step make sense? is this measurement right?), then recalls the ingredients in order or in reverse - a verbal/numeric complex span.
interaction: Each cycle shows a processing check answered true/false - toggle among READ (does a short pictured or spoken step make sense), OPERATION (is a simple measurement right, e.g. 2 cups plus 1 cup makes 3 cups), COUNT (is the tally correct) and SYMMETRY/ROTATE (is the plating mirrored, or which way the utensil points) - then briefly shows an ingredient to remember. After N cycles the child taps the ingredients back in presentation order, with a Reverse-recall toggle that asks for them in reverse (a backward span under load). Set size adapts up on perfect recall with accurate processing; processing is time-limited.
self_teach: The ghost-hand marks a sensible step true, an ingredient appears, one more cycle follows, then it taps the two ingredients back in order with a check mark (about 9s); one unscored warm-up follows. A large check and cross plus the ingredient tray teach the rhythm with no reading required in the demo.

learning_science.principle: Reading span and the processing-storage trade-off
learning_science.why: Interleaving comprehension with storage is the classic complex-span predictor of higher-order verbal ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a sensibility judgment as the processing task while holding ingredients for ordered recall.
learning_science.source: Daneman, M., & Carpenter, P. A. (1980). Individual differences in working memory and reading. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 19(4), 450-466.

learning_science.why: Standardized operation span (verify a simple computation plus storage) is a reliable individual-difference measure of WM capacity.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer an operation module (verify a simple measurement) as an alternate processing task.
learning_science.source: Unsworth, N., Heitz, R. P., Schrock, J. C., & Engle, R. W. (2005). An automated version of the operation span task. Behavior Research Methods, 37(3), 498-505.

learning_science.why: Recalling the held set in reverse taxes manipulation beyond storage, lifting the ceiling for older children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Add a reverse-recall toggle so the same shell yields a manipulation contrast (backward digit span under load).
learning_science.source: Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), The Psychology of Learning and Motivation (Vol. 8, pp. 47-89). Academic Press.

tail_precision_rationale: A verbal or numeric processing task interleaved with ordered storage indexes executive attention: adaptive recall span (M-SPAN, M-DIFFREACH) is an above-grade capacity index, position partial-credit (M-POLY) grades each recall, processing accuracy (M-PROCACC) gates validity against speed-accuracy trade-offs, and intrusion-lure typing (M-LURETYPE) with order-vs-item error typing (M-ERRTYPE) exposes proactive-interference control; the reverse-recall toggle adds a manipulation contrast that lifts the ceiling, while first-move latency (M-RTFIRST) is logged as process only.
age_rationale: The reading and operation modules require basic literacy and numeracy, so the honest floor is 4-5 (matching operation-span and backward-digit items at 4-5) and scales to reading span and reverse recall at 6-8; it is not used pre-reading, so K-1 is excluded. Responses are taps only.

adaptive.content_range: 4-5 operation span at set size 2 with forward recall up to 6-8 reading span with reverse recall at set sizes 4-5
adaptive.difficulty_levers: set size, processing module and time limit, forward vs reverse recall, lure similarity of the memoranda
adaptive.notes: Processing items and memoranda are generated and set size is a native staircase; the processing-accuracy gate must be enforced.

engagement_hook: A cooking-line game where you fact-check each step then remember the ingredients in order, like keeping a busy recipe straight in your head.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Academic skill: reading and operation modules confound with literacy and numeracy, so processing accuracy is reported separately and the type is reserved for 4-5 and up. Attention/ADHD: dual-tasking amplifies attention, so gate on M-PROCACC and engagement. Speed-accuracy trade-off is detected by M-PROCACC. Motor/familiarity: large tray targets and a warm-up. Language: spoken steps have picture equivalents so the demo is reading-free.

name: Signal Radar (dual n-back / updating)
one_liner: Blips sweep a radar scope while tones or letters play, and the child flags when the current position (or sound) matches the one n sweeps back, or keeps a running value or tally that must be updated.
interaction: In n-back mode a blip appears on the scope each sweep and the child taps WHERE-MATCH when the current position equals the one n sweeps back; dual mode adds a letter channel with a separate WHAT-MATCH button and the child responds to either channel. A numeric-updating shell shows a running value changed by occasional operations and probes the current value; a symbol-counter shell requires separate running tallies of two or more blip types, reported on demand. Responses do not advance the sweep; n or update load rises at high sensitivity and falls at low.
self_teach: A wordless 1-back demo shows two blips in the same spot one sweep apart and the hand tapping WHERE-MATCH with a check mark (about 7s), then an unscored 1-back warm-up; the sweep rhythm and the match button read instantly with no text.

learning_science.principle: N-back as a continuous updating measure
learning_science.why: The n-back requires constant encoding, monitoring and replacement of WM contents and correlates with fluid reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a continuous sweep with a MATCH judgment and an adaptive n level.
learning_science.source: Kirchner, W. K. (1958). Age differences in short-term retention of rapidly changing information. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 55(4), 352-358.

learning_science.why: Adding a second modality stream increases domain-general updating demand and lifts the ceiling for older children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a dual spatial-plus-verbal mode with separate response buttons per channel.
learning_science.source: Jaeggi, S. M., Buschkuehl, M., Jonides, J., & Perrig, W. J. (2008). Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 105(19), 6829-6833.

learning_science.why: Hits and false alarms confound ability with response bias unless modeled with sensitivity.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score with d-prime and flag lure false alarms rather than raw hit counts.
learning_science.source: Green, D. M., & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley.

tail_precision_rationale: A continuous dual-channel updating task is rich in process telemetry: signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) separates true match detection from response bias, the highest sustained n and update load (M-DIFFREACH) probe capacity above grade level, lure (n plus or minus 1) false alarms (M-ERRTYPE) reveal fragile temporal binding, the accuracy-by-load slope (M-UPDATECOST) indexes updating efficiency, and RT variability and lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) with drift and engagement gating (M-DRIFT, M-ENGAGE) score worst-performance consistency rather than impulsive speed.
age_rationale: Continuous updating with response withholding is too demanding and attention-confounded for most K-1 children, so the floor is 2-3 (single 1-back), moving to 2-back and numeric updating at 4-5 and 2-3-back, dual-channel and multi-counter shells at 6-8. Only one or two large buttons are tapped, and the numeric and counter shells assume counting so they are age-gated to 4-5 and up.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 single 1-back up to 6-8 dual (spatial plus verbal) n-back, numeric running-value and multi-symbol-counter updating
adaptive.difficulty_levers: n level, single vs dual channel, sweep pace, target and lure rate, update step size, number of counters
adaptive.notes: Sweeps, tones, operations and probe schedules are generated with controlled target and lure rates, and n and update load are native staircases.

engagement_hook: A sonar-scope arcade where you flag repeating blips and keep the count straight; speeding sweeps and dual channels make leveling up feel like manning mission control.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention/ADHD is the dominant confound: continuous updating loads sustained attention and impulse control, so d-prime (bias-free) is reported, drift and engagement are tracked across the sweep, consistency is weighted over speed, and scores are gated on engaged blocks. Numeracy: numeric and counter shells need counting and are age-gated. Motor: a fixed sweep may clip slow responses, mitigated by a generous response window. Familiarity: novelty is mitigated by the warm-up. Audio: the WHAT channel uses visible letters so audio is not required.

name: Bubble Pop Memory (n-back / dual n-back)
one_liner: Bubbles float up one at a time showing a picture, and the child taps POP whenever the current bubble matches the one from n bubbles ago; a dual mode adds a sound channel.
interaction: Bubbles rise at a fixed pace, each showing a shape or colour; the child taps a POP button when the current bubble equals the one n steps back (single stream). Dual mode plays a chime or shows a letter alongside each bubble with a separate SOUND-POP button, and the child responds to either channel independently. Taps do not advance the stream. n rises when signal-detection sensitivity is high (about 80 percent) and falls when it is low, pushing each child above grade level; scoring is sensitivity- and consistency-based, never raw speed.
self_teach: A wordless 1-back ghost-hand demo shows two identical bubbles in a row and the hand tapping POP with a check (about 6s), then an unscored 1-back warm-up; the rising-bubble rhythm and the POP button read instantly with no text.

learning_science.principle: N-back as a continuous updating measure
learning_science.why: The n-back requires constant encoding, monitoring, and replacement of working-memory contents and correlates with fluid reasoning, giving a high ceiling as n rises.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a continuous rising-bubble stream with a POP judgment and an adaptive n level that escalates above grade.
learning_science.source: Kirchner, W. K. (1958). Age differences in short-term retention of rapidly changing information. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 55(4), 352-358.

learning_science.why: Adding a second modality stream raises domain-general updating demand and lifts the ceiling for older children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a dual visual-plus-auditory mode with separate response buttons per channel for the 6-8 band.
learning_science.source: Jaeggi, S. M., Buschkuehl, M., Jonides, J., & Perrig, W. J. (2008). Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 105(19), 6829-6833.

learning_science.why: Hits and false alarms confound ability with response bias unless modeled with sensitivity, so consistency and d-prime rather than hit count define the score.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score with d-prime and flag lure (n plus or minus 1) false alarms rather than crediting fast taps.
learning_science.source: Green, D. M., & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley.

tail_precision_rationale: A continuous updating stream is rich in tail telemetry: signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) separates true match detection from response bias, lure false alarms (M-FALSEALARM at n plus or minus 1) expose fragile temporal binding, the accuracy-by-load slope (M-UPDATECOST) indexes updating efficiency, and the highest sustained n (M-DIFFREACH) probes capacity above grade level; RT variability (M-RTVAR) scores worst-performance consistency rather than impulsive speed.
age_rationale: Continuous updating with response withholding is too demanding for most K-1 children, so the floor is 2-3 (single 1-back at a gentle pace), rising to 2-3-back at 4-5 and dual-channel n-back at 6-8. Only one or two large buttons are tapped and the sound channel has a visible letter fallback so audio is not required.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 single 1-back at a gentle pace up to 6-8 dual visual-plus-auditory n-back at higher n
adaptive.difficulty_levers: n level; single versus dual channel; bubble pace; target and lure rate
adaptive.notes: Bubble streams, tones, and lure schedules are generated with controlled target and lure rates, and n is a native above-grade staircase.

engagement_hook: A bubble-popping arcade where you pop only the bubbles that repeat from n-ago; faster streams and a second sound channel make leveling up feel like a real challenge.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD are the dominant confound: continuous updating loads sustained attention and impulse control, so bias-free d-prime is reported, consistency is weighted over speed, and scores are gated on engaged blocks. A fixed pace can clip slow responses (generous response window). Novelty is mitigated by the warm-up. The auditory channel uses a visible letter so muted or deaf and hard-of-hearing children are not disadvantaged.

name: Freeze Dance (go/no-go, stop-signal, statue)
one_liner: Tap the dancer on every beat, but freeze and do not tap when the music stops or the statue light shows; if you already started to tap when freeze flashes, pull back - and hold still through the statue round.
interaction: Go trials: a character dances and the child taps on the beat (frequent, prepotent). No-go trials: a statue light or the music stopping means withhold. Stop-signal trials: a go begins but turns red after a variable delay that tracks up after successful stops and down after failures (a staircase) to estimate stop-signal reaction time. A statue round asks the child to keep hands off for a few seconds while distractor sounds and wiggles try to provoke a tap (motor hold). Real response times are recorded but scoring rewards control and consistency, not speed.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps to two beats (checks), then visibly pulls back and freezes when the statue light shows (about 7s); an unscored warm-up block follows. Dance-versus-freeze reads instantly with no text.

learning_science.why: A high go rate builds a prepotent tapping response that must be actively withheld on no-go trials, isolating response inhibition from speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep go frequent and no-go rare, and titrate inhibitory load by no-go probability and pace.
learning_science.source: Simpson, A., & Riggs, K. J. (2006). Conditions under which children experience inhibitory difficulty with a go/no-go task. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 94(1), 18-26.

learning_science.why: Cancelling an already-initiated response estimates the latency of the covert inhibitory process, one of the least coachable executive metrics.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Stagger the stop delay with a staircase and estimate SSRT as median go RT minus mean stop-signal delay.
learning_science.source: Logan, G. D., & Cowan, W. B. (1984). On the ability to inhibit thought and action: A theory of an act of control. Psychological Review, 91(3), 295-327.

learning_science.why: Holding a still posture while resisting distractors is a developmentally sensitive child motor-inhibition measure that complements button-press inhibition.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include a timed statue hold with distractors and log premature taps as motor-inhibition failures.
learning_science.source: Korkman, M., Kirk, U., & Kemp, S. (2007). NEPSY-II: Statue subtest. Pearson.

tail_precision_rationale: Three inhibition demands share one shell: commission errors on no-go and statue trials (M-COMM) index prepotent-response control, the staircased stop-signal reaction time (M-SSRT) is a continuous, hard-to-coach latency of covert inhibition, false alarms and anticipatory taps (M-FALSEALARM) isolate impulsive responding, and post-error slowing (M-POSTERR) indexes performance monitoring; RT variability (M-RTVAR) and engagement gating (M-ENGAGE) score sustained control rather than peak speed at the cut.
age_rationale: Tap-on-beat with a freeze is intuitive from K-1 (the statue and simple go/no-go shells), while the stop-signal cancel and faster, rarer no-go trials add above-grade difficulty through 6-8. Responses are large-area taps or withholding, with no reading; the beat and lights carry the task.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 slow go/no-go and statue holds up to 6-8 fast staircased stop-signal with rare, quick no-go trials
adaptive.difficulty_levers: no-go probability; beat pace; stop-signal delay (staircased); statue-hold duration and distractor intensity
adaptive.notes: Beat schedules, no-go placement, and stop delays are generated; SSRT needs enough stop trials and the statue hold needs a fixed distractor script.

engagement_hook: A freeze-dance party: groove on every beat then freeze like a statue when the music cuts - staying frozen while everything tries to make you move feels like a real test of cool.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD amplify commission errors, so consistency (M-RTVAR) and engagement (M-ENGAGE) gate tail calls and bias-controlled metrics are reported. Motor and device: large tap areas and a generous window; premature statue taps are logged separately from go/no-go. Rhythm or hearing differences are mitigated by a visible beat and statue light so audio is not required. Novelty is handled by the ghost-hand and warm-up.

name: Launch Control (go/no-go, stop-signal, statue)
one_liner: Tap to launch friendly rockets fast, never launch a bomb, and if the abort light flashes after you commit, cancel the launch - plus a countdown pose you must hold still.
interaction: Go trials: a friendly rocket sits on the pad and the child taps LAUNCH quickly (frequent). No-go trials: a bomb appears and the child must withhold. Stop-signal trials: after a launch is initiated a red ABORT light appears at a variable, staircased delay and the child must cancel (a pull-back animation), estimating stop-signal reaction time. A hold-steady countdown round requires no taps while distractors flash. An accuracy-gated combo grows only on correct and controlled responses and resets on any error, false alarm, or premature tap, so speed is credited only when accuracy is held.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps LAUNCH on two rockets (checks), withholds on a bomb, then starts a launch and pulls back when the red ABORT light flashes (about 8s); an unscored warm-up follows. Launch-versus-hold reads instantly with no text.

learning_science.why: Aborting a committed action models the race between going and stopping and yields SSRT, a continuous latent inhibition metric with strong high-end resolution.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Initiate a go then present a staircased stop signal and estimate SSRT from the go-RT distribution and stop-signal delay.
learning_science.source: Verbruggen, F., & Logan, G. D. (2008). Response inhibition in the stop-signal paradigm. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 12(11), 418-424.

learning_science.why: A high launch rate builds a prepotent response so withholding on rare bombs isolates inhibitory control from processing speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep launches frequent and bombs rare and titrate no-go probability and pacing.
learning_science.source: Simpson, A., & Riggs, K. J. (2006). Conditions under which children experience inhibitory difficulty with a go/no-go task. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 94(1), 18-26.

learning_science.why: A child's slowest and least controlled responses, not the fastest, are most diagnostic of ability, so speed is only rewarded when accuracy is sustained.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score a combo streak that requires both correctness and a controlled response and reset it on any lapse, and hold a countdown pose to index motor control.
learning_science.source: Coyle, T. R. (2003). A review of the worst performance rule: Evidence, theory, and alternative hypotheses. Intelligence, 31(6), 567-587.

tail_precision_rationale: The abort mechanic centers a hard-to-coach latent metric: stop-signal reaction time (M-SSRT) resolves the high end continuously, commission errors on bombs (M-COMM) and false alarms or anticipations (M-FALSEALARM) isolate impulsive responding, post-error slowing (M-POSTERR) indexes monitoring, and the accuracy-gated combo (M-COMBO) credits sustained joint speed-and-accuracy rather than impulsive peak speed; raw RT (M-RT) is logged only as process behind the gate.
age_rationale: Tap-to-launch and withhold-on-bomb work from K-1 (the go/no-go and hold shells), while the staircased abort and faster, rarer bombs give above-grade difficulty through 6-8. Responses are large taps or withholding with no reading; rocket and bomb icons carry the task.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 slow go/no-go with rare bombs up to 6-8 fast staircased stop-signal aborts with tight timing
adaptive.difficulty_levers: bomb (no-go) probability; launch pace; abort-signal delay (staircased); countdown-hold duration and distractor intensity
adaptive.notes: Trial schedules and abort delays are generated; SSRT needs enough abort trials and the combo needs a per-child adaptive RT band.

engagement_hook: A mission-control launch game: fire the good rockets fast but slam the abort when a launch goes wrong - keeping a clean streak feels like being the calmest hand in the control room.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD amplify commissions and anticipations, so the accuracy-gated combo, false-alarm rate, and consistency gate tail calls rather than raw speed. Motor and device latency inflate RT and SSRT, mitigated by a generous window and by reporting SSRT (which subtracts baseline) plus a controlled-response gate. Impulsive fast-wrong responding is caught by M-FALSEALARM. Novelty is handled by the ghost-hand and warm-up.

name: Middle Muddle (flanker / conflict / switch)
one_liner: Point to which way the middle creature faces while ignoring its neighbors; sometimes the rule flips to which side is truly bigger in number, or name the ink not the word, so you must switch.
interaction: A row of creatures or arrows appears and the child taps the direction the center one faces, ignoring congruent or incongruent flankers (flanker interference). A numeric shell shows two number-critters that differ in physical size and value and the child taps the one that is truly larger in number, ignoring size (numerical Stroop). A switch shell alternates between naming the ink colour and reading the colour word, cued by a small icon, forcing rule switches. Response times and accuracy are logged by congruency and by switch versus repeat; scoring credits interference control and consistency, not raw speed.
self_teach: The ghost-hand shows an incongruent row (center faces right, neighbors face left) and taps the center direction with a check (about 6s); an unscored warm-up follows. Only-the-middle reads instantly from the highlight and demo.

learning_science.why: Flanking distractors that conflict with the target require selective attention and response inhibition; the incongruent-minus-congruent cost isolates interference control from baseline speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present congruent, incongruent, and neutral flankers around a central target and score the congruency effect.
learning_science.source: Eriksen, B. A., & Eriksen, C. W. (1974). Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task. Perception & Psychophysics, 16(1), 143-149.

learning_science.why: When physical size conflicts with numeric value, judging value while suppressing size indexes interference control and taps automatic magnitude processing, extending discrimination for numerate older children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include a size-value conflict shell scored by the interference cost, with a dot-quantity variant for pre-numeric young children.
learning_science.source: Henik, A., & Tzelgov, J. (1982). Is three greater than five: The relation between physical and semantic size in comparison tasks. Memory & Cognition, 10(4), 389-395.

learning_science.why: Alternating between two rules (ink versus word) incurs a switch cost that indexes set-shifting efficiency separate from interference control.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Interleave ink-naming and word-reading cued trial-by-trial and score switch minus repeat cost.
learning_science.source: Monsell, S. (2003). Task switching. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 7(3), 134-140.

tail_precision_rationale: Interference and switching are decomposed on one shell: the congruency effect (M-CONGEFF) isolates interference control independent of baseline speed, the switch cost (M-SWITCHCOST) indexes set-shifting, and the accuracy-gated combo (M-COMBO) with RT variability (M-RTVAR) and post-error slowing (M-POSTERR) credit sustained controlled processing rather than impulsive peak speed; a small congruency and switch cost held at high accuracy is a strong, hard-to-game tail marker.
age_rationale: Point-to-the-middle flanker works from K-1 (large creatures, single tap), while the numeric-conflict and ink-word switch shells and faster pacing add above-grade difficulty through 6-8; the numerical shell uses dot quantities for pre-numeric young children and digits for older. No reading is required for the flanker and dot shells; the word shell is age-gated to readers.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 slow flanker with large creatures up to 6-8 mixed flanker, numerical-conflict, and ink-word switching at pace
adaptive.difficulty_levers: flanker congruency and spacing; size-value conflict magnitude; switch rate and cue transparency; response pace
adaptive.notes: Rows, conflicts, and switch schedules are generated with controlled congruency and switch rates; enough trials per condition are needed for stable congruency and switch costs.

engagement_hook: A spotlight game where only the middle critter matters until the rule flips on you; keeping your cool when everything around it points the wrong way feels like true focus.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD inflate interference and switch costs, so consistency (M-RTVAR) and accuracy gating are weighted over speed. Numeracy confounds the numeric shell (dot-quantity variant for young; digits age-gated). Reading confounds the ink-word shell (age-gated to readers; flanker and dot shells are reading-free). Colour vision is aided by distinct hues plus shape redundancy. Motor and familiarity are handled by large taps and the warm-up.

name: True Tug (numerical Stroop / conflict tug)
one_liner: Pull the rope toward the side that is truly bigger in number, ignoring how large or crowded it looks; sometimes ignore the surrounding distractors or switch to naming the ink not the word.
interaction: A tug-of-war rope sits between two sides that each show a quantity or a digit; the physical size or crowding conflicts with the true numeric value and the child taps or drags toward the side that is numerically greater (numerical Stroop). A flanker variant surrounds the target quantity with distractor items to ignore, and a switch variant alternates between naming the ink colour of a word and reading the word, cued by an icon. For pre-numeric young children the sides show dot quantities whose dot size conflicts with count. Congruency and switch costs, error type, and consistency are logged; scoring credits conflict control, not speed.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sees a small-looking 8 beside a big-looking 3 and pulls the rope toward the 8 with a check (about 6s); an unscored warm-up follows. Pull-the-bigger-number reads instantly from the demo with no text.

learning_science.why: Judging numeric value while suppressing conflicting physical size indexes interference control and automatic magnitude access, a size-value conflict cost that extends discrimination for numerate children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Vary the congruency of physical size and numeric value and score the interference cost, with a dot-count-versus-dot-size variant for pre-numeric children.
learning_science.source: Henik, A., & Tzelgov, J. (1982). Is three greater than five: The relation between physical and semantic size in comparison tasks. Memory & Cognition, 10(4), 389-395.

learning_science.why: For pre-numeric young children, comparing quantities while ignoring size probes non-symbolic magnitude acuity, a low-literacy signal that keeps separating children before symbols are known.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a non-symbolic dot-quantity tug for K-1 in which dot size conflicts with count, adapting the ratio.
learning_science.source: Halberda, J., Mazzocco, M. M. M., & Feigenson, L. (2008). Individual differences in non-verbal number acuity correlate with maths achievement. Nature, 455(7213), 665-668.

learning_science.why: Alternating between ink-naming and word-reading incurs a switch cost that indexes set-shifting separate from magnitude interference.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Interleave an ink-versus-word rule cued trial-by-trial and score switch minus repeat cost.
learning_science.source: Monsell, S. (2003). Task switching. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 7(3), 134-140.

tail_precision_rationale: The tug isolates magnitude interference: the congruency effect (M-CONGEFF) is the size-value conflict cost independent of baseline speed, error typing (M-ERRTYPE: captured by size versus a genuine magnitude slip) reveals whether near-misses are interference capture or true confusion, the switch cost (M-SWITCHCOST) adds a set-shifting axis, and RT variability (M-RTVAR) with the accuracy-gated combo (M-COMBO) credit sustained control over impulsive speed at the cut.
age_rationale: The non-symbolic dot-quantity tug works from K-1 (compare which side has more, ignore size, single tap or drag), while symbolic digit conflict and the ink-word switch add above-grade difficulty for numerate, reading older children through 6-8. The dot shell is reading- and number-free; the digit and word shells are age-gated.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 non-symbolic dot-quantity tug (size conflicts with count) up to 6-8 symbolic digit size-value conflict with an ink-word switch
adaptive.difficulty_levers: size-value conflict magnitude; numeric or ratio distance; presence of flankers; switch rate; response pace
adaptive.notes: Sides, conflicts, ratios, and switch schedules are generated with controlled congruency; enough trials per condition are needed for stable congruency and switch costs.

engagement_hook: A tug-of-war where the bigger number wins the rope, not the bigger-looking one; refusing to be fooled by size makes the win feel earned.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Numeracy confounds the digit shell (dot-quantity variant for young; digits age-gated), and the ink-word switch confounds reading (age-gated to readers). Attention and ADHD inflate the conflict cost, so consistency (M-RTVAR) and accuracy gating are weighted over speed. Colour vision uses distinct hues plus shape or numeral redundancy. Motor and familiarity are handled by large targets, tap-or-drag, and the warm-up.

name: Secret Rule Zoo (rule-discovery sort / intra-extra shift)
one_liner: Send each animal to the gate it likes; the secret rule (colour, shape, or how many) must be worked out from happy or sad feedback, and it changes without warning.
interaction: Each animal card has several features (colour, shape, count). The child sends it to one of two gates and gets happy or sad feedback; the sorting rule is unstated and must be discovered from feedback (Wisconsin-style). After a run of correct sorts the rule silently changes, requiring a shift. An intra-extra staging first rewards one value in a dimension, then shifts to another value in the same dimension (intra-dimensional) and later to a new dimension (extra-dimensional). Perseverative errors, trials to criterion, hypothesis-search efficiency, and rule dimensionality are logged; scoring credits flexible rule updating and strategy, not speed.
self_teach: The ghost-hand tries one gate, gets a sad face, moves the next animal to the other gate for a happy face, and keeps using the winning gate until it stops working (about 8s); an unscored warm-up follows. Discover-the-rule-from-faces self-teaches with no text.

learning_science.why: Discovering an unstated sorting rule from feedback and shifting when it changes indexes cognitive flexibility, with perseverative errors marking failure to update the set.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Hide the rule, give only correct or incorrect feedback, and change the rule after a success run, logging perseverative errors.
learning_science.source: Grant, D. A., & Berg, E. A. (1948). A behavioral analysis of degree of reinforcement and ease of shifting to new responses in a Weigl-type card-sorting problem. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 38(4), 404-411.

learning_science.why: Shifting to a new value within the same dimension is easier than shifting to a new dimension, and the extra-dimensional cost is a fine-grained flexibility marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Stage reversals within a dimension then across dimensions and report the extra-dimensional shift cost separately.
learning_science.source: Roberts, A. C., Robbins, T. W., & Everitt, B. J. (1988). The effects of intradimensional and extradimensional shifts on visual discrimination learning in humans and non-human primates. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology B, 40(4), 321-341.

learning_science.why: Efficient rule discovery runs informative, disambiguating tests rather than random or perseverative ones, indexing inductive reasoning and learning rate.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log the reduction in the viable-rule space per sort to score hypothesis-search efficiency.
learning_science.source: Bruner, J. S., Goodnow, J. J., & Austin, G. A. (1956). A Study of Thinking. Wiley.

tail_precision_rationale: Feedback-driven discovery exposes flexibility that cued sorts miss: the perseverative-error rate (M-PERSEV) directly indexes failure to update after a silent rule change, hypothesis-search efficiency (M-HYP) captures how quickly a child converges via disambiguating sorts, rule dimensionality solved (M-RULEID) grades how many co-acting features the child integrates, and the extra-dimensional shift cost (M-SWITCHCOST) with the full sort path (M-PATH) separates flexible high-ability sorters at the cut; scoring is strategy- and accuracy-based rather than speed.
age_rationale: Discovering a hidden rule from feedback is beyond most K-1 children, so the floor is 2-3 with a single-dimension rule and generous feedback, rising to multi-feature cards, silent rule changes, and extra-dimensional shifts at 6-8 (above grade). Sorting is a single large-target tap or drag with no reading; feedback is faces, not words.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 one-dimension rule with obvious feedback up to 6-8 multi-feature cards with silent rule changes and extra-dimensional shifts
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of features per card; how silently and how often the rule changes; intra- versus extra-dimensional shifts; feedback delay
adaptive.notes: Cards, rules, and shift schedules are generated; hypothesis-search efficiency and rule dimensionality need distractor features orthogonally keyed to individual rules.

engagement_hook: A zookeeper mystery: figure out the animals secret rule from happy and sad faces, then keep up when the rule sneakily changes - cracking each new rule fast feels clever.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD affect feedback tracking, so strategy metrics and consistency gate tail calls. Working-memory load of holding the current hypothesis is intrinsic to the construct but supported by a visible feedback history. Colour vision uses distinct hues plus shape and count redundancy so rules are never colour-only. Motor and familiarity are handled by large targets and the warm-up; a response bias for one gate is controlled by balancing correct-gate placement.

name: Costume Party (DCCS match-to-sample / switch)
one_liner: Match each guest to the target guest by the rule in play - first by costume colour, then the rule switches to hat shape - a match-to-sample card switch.
interaction: A guest card showing both a colour and a shape appears with two target guests; the child taps the target that matches on the current dimension (match-to-sample DCCS). Several trials sort by colour, then the rule switches to shape (standard DCCS); a border or badge cue variant signals the rule trial-by-trial for rapid switching; an intra-extra variant changes which value or dimension is relevant. Response times and accuracy are logged by switch versus repeat and by congruency; scoring credits switch efficiency and low perseveration, not speed.
self_teach: The ghost-hand matches a blue-hat guest to the blue target under a colour badge (check), then after the badge changes to shape matches by hat shape (about 7s); an unscored warm-up follows. Match-by-the-current-badge self-teaches with no text.

learning_science.why: Sorting by one dimension then switching to another is a standard, developmentally sensitive measure of cognitive flexibility in young children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a match-to-sample DCCS with a pre-switch, post-switch, and a border-cued mixed phase.
learning_science.source: Zelazo, P. D. (2006). The Dimensional Change Card Sort (DCCS): A method of assessing executive function in children. Nature Protocols, 1(1), 297-301.

learning_science.principle: Set-shifting as a separable executive function
learning_science.why: Shifting between task sets is a distinct executive component whose cost (switch minus repeat) indexes flexibility beyond inhibition and updating.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score switch cost from mixed trials and report it separately from accuracy.
learning_science.source: Miyake, A., Friedman, N. P., Emerson, M. J., Witzki, A. H., Howerter, A., & Wager, T. D. (2000). The unity and diversity of executive functions. Cognitive Psychology, 41(1), 49-100.

learning_science.principle: Conflict and attentional inertia in switching
learning_science.why: Post-switch errors reflect attentional inertia to the old dimension, so bivalent (colour and shape) cards create the conflict that discriminates flexible children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use bivalent cards so post-switch perseveration and congruency effects are measurable.
learning_science.source: Diamond, A. (2013). Executive functions. Annual Review of Psychology, 64, 135-168.

tail_precision_rationale: A match-to-sample switch cleanly decomposes flexibility: the switch cost (M-SWITCHCOST) indexes reconfiguration, perseverative errors (M-PERSEV) capture attentional inertia to the old dimension after a switch, the congruency effect (M-CONGEFF) on bivalent cards indexes conflict control, and low RT variability (M-RTVAR) with adaptive post-error slowing (M-POSTERR) marks flexible high-ability switchers holding accuracy rather than trading it for speed at the cut.
age_rationale: The standard DCCS is calibrated for early childhood, so the floor is 2-3 (pre- and post-switch by one dimension), rising to border-cued rapid switching and intra-extra shifts at 4-5 and 6-8 (above grade). Matching is a single large-target tap with no reading; badges are icons, not words.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 pre/post-switch by one dimension up to 6-8 border-cued rapid mixed switching with intra-extra shifts
adaptive.difficulty_levers: switch frequency; cue transparency (blocked versus trial-by-trial badge); congruency of the bivalent cards; intra- versus extra-dimensional shift; pace
adaptive.notes: Guests, targets, and switch schedules are generated; the switch cost needs enough switch and repeat trials and bivalent cards for congruency.

engagement_hook: A costume party where you match guests by the rule on the badge, then the rule changes and you have to keep up; nailing the switch without slipping into the old rule feels sharp.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD inflate switch and perseveration costs, so consistency and accuracy gate tail calls. Colour vision is aided by distinct hues plus shape redundancy (the two dimensions are colour and shape so neither is essential alone across trials). Reading is avoided by icon badges. Motor and familiarity are handled by large taps and the warm-up; a side bias is controlled by randomising target positions.

name: New Every Time (self-ordered pointing)
one_liner: Each turn, tap a picture you have not tapped before - but the pictures shuffle their positions every turn, so you must remember which ones you picked, not where they were.
interaction: An array of distinct pictures is shown and each turn the child must tap one that has not been chosen before; after each choice the positions reshuffle so location cannot be used as a crutch. Tapping a previously chosen picture is a between-selection error. The set grows when a round is completed cleanly (above grade). The self-generated selection sequence, between-selection errors, and strategy are logged; scoring is error- and strategy-based, never speed.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps one picture, the array reshuffles, and it taps a different picture, avoiding the first, with a check (about 7s); an unscored warm-up follows. Pick-a-new-one-each-time self-teaches through the reshuffle and demo.

learning_science.why: Choosing a not-yet-chosen item each turn requires maintaining and updating a self-generated record of prior choices, a frontal working-memory monitoring task distinct from experimenter-ordered span.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require a new choice each turn and reshuffle positions so identity, not location, must be tracked.
learning_science.source: Petrides, M., & Milner, B. (1982). Deficits on subject-ordered tasks after frontal- and temporal-lobe lesions in man. Neuropsychologia, 20(3), 249-262.

learning_science.why: Efficient performers impose a systematic strategy on self-ordered search, and strategy predicts ability beyond error counts.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log the selection sequence and score a strategy index alongside between-selection errors.
learning_science.source: Owen, A. M., Downes, J. J., Sahakian, B. J., Polkey, C. E., & Robbins, T. W. (1990). Planning and spatial working memory following frontal lobe lesions in man. Neuropsychologia, 28(10), 1021-1034.

learning_science.why: Maintaining a growing set of already-chosen items pushes against the capacity limit, so a growing set size maximises information at the tail.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Grow the array size after clean rounds to probe capacity above grade level.
learning_science.source: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87-114.

tail_precision_rationale: Position shuffling forces identity-based monitoring: between-selection errors (M-BETWEENERR) index failure to maintain and update the self-generated record, the strategy score (M-SEARCHSTRAT) with the selection path (M-PATH) reveals planful self-ordering, and the largest clean set size (M-DIFFREACH) is an above-grade capacity index; revisions (M-REV) separate slips from genuine memory failures, scoring capacity and strategy rather than speed at the cut.
age_rationale: Pick-a-new-one is intuitive from K-1 with a small array of familiar pictures and a single tap; growing arrays and faster reshuffles give above-grade difficulty through 6-8. No reading and one tap per turn; the reshuffle removes any location crutch so the load is memory, not motor.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 small arrays of 3-4 familiar pictures up to 6-8 large arrays of 8-plus with faster reshuffles
adaptive.difficulty_levers: array size; reshuffle speed; visual similarity of the pictures; optional retention delay between turns
adaptive.notes: Picture sets and reshuffle schedules are generated and array size is a native above-grade staircase; enough turns per set size are needed for stable between-error and strategy estimates.

engagement_hook: A memory game where the pictures keep dancing to new spots and you must always pick a fresh one; tracking who you have already chosen feels like outsmarting the shuffle.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD affect self-monitoring, so consistency and strategy gate tail calls. Location as a crutch is removed by reshuffling so the construct is identity-based monitoring. Colour vision uses distinct, nameable pictures. Motor and familiarity are handled by large targets, a single tap per turn, and the warm-up; impulsive re-taps are logged as revisions so slips are not scored as memory errors.

name: Dino Dig (self-ordered spatial search)
one_liner: Dig holes to find hidden fossils; once a hole gives a fossil it is empty, so never dig that winning hole again - and do not re-dig a hole this round that you already found empty.
interaction: A field of dig-spots is shown and the child taps to dig; one fossil is hidden per hunt. A spot that has already yielded a fossil is exhausted, so returning to it later is a between-search error, and re-digging a spot found empty within the current hunt is a within-search revision. After each find a new fossil is hidden until every spot has produced one; the number of spots grows when play is clean (above grade). Between-search errors, search strategy, efficiency, and persistence are logged; scoring credits strategy and consistency, not speed.
self_teach: The ghost-hand digs one empty spot, then a fossil spot, collects it, and does not dig that spot again (about 7s); an unscored warm-up hunt follows. The exhausted-spot rule self-teaches through the collect animation and demo.

learning_science.why: Searching boxes for hidden tokens without revisiting exhausted ones taxes spatial working-memory maintenance and updating across searches, with between-search errors as the key index.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Hide one token at a time and count returns to already-exhausted spots as between-search errors.
learning_science.source: Owen, A. M., Downes, J. J., Sahakian, B. J., Polkey, C. E., & Robbins, T. W. (1990). Planning and spatial working memory following frontal lobe lesions in man. Neuropsychologia, 28(10), 1021-1034.

learning_science.why: Following a fixed, systematic search sequence (few distinct starting spots) reveals planful strategy that predicts ability beyond raw error counts.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score a strategy index from how consistently the child begins each new search from the same spot and log the full move path.
learning_science.source: Robbins, T. W., James, M., Owen, A. M., Sahakian, B. J., McInnes, L., & Rabbitt, P. (1994). Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB). Dementia, 5(5), 266-281.

learning_science.why: Maintaining a self-generated record of which spots have been visited within and across searches is the frontal monitoring demand that separates strong performers.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distinguish within-search revisits from across-search returns to separate transient slips from monitoring failures.
learning_science.source: Petrides, M., & Milner, B. (1982). Deficits on subject-ordered tasks after frontal- and temporal-lobe lesions in man. Neuropsychologia, 20(3), 249-262.

tail_precision_rationale: Self-ordered search yields executive process signals span tasks miss: between-search errors (M-BETWEENERR) index failure to maintain and update the spatial record across searches, the strategy score (M-SEARCHSTRAT) captures planful systematic sweeping, efficiency versus the optimal search (M-EFF) with the full move path (M-PATH) separates economical solvers, and the largest clean field (M-DIFFREACH) is an above-grade capacity index; persistence on large fields (M-PERSIST) adds task-commitment signal, all scored on strategy and consistency rather than speed.
age_rationale: Dig-and-collect is intuitive from K-1 with a few spots and a single tap; larger fields and more concurrent exhausted spots give above-grade difficulty through 6-8. No reading and one tap per dig; the collect animation makes the exhausted-spot rule obvious so the load is memory, not motor.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 fields of 3-4 spots up to 6-8 fields of 8-plus spots with denser layouts
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of spots; spatial layout density; optional delay between searches; whether exhausted spots stay visually marked
adaptive.notes: Fields and hiding schedules are generated and spot count is a native above-grade staircase; the strategy score needs higher set sizes and several rounds for stability.

engagement_hook: A paleontology dig where each fossil you unearth empties its hole for good; sweeping the field without ever wasting a dig on an old spot feels like a real expert hunt.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD affect search monitoring, so strategy and consistency gate tail calls and within-search slips are separated from between-search monitoring failures. Location memory is the target construct; spots are large and well-spaced so motor mis-taps are minimised and logged as revisions. Colour vision is not required (spots are neutral). Familiarity is handled by the ghost-hand and warm-up.

name: Critter Pop (peek-a-boo 1-back + hideout span)
one_liner: Big animals peek out of burrows one at a time and the child slaps a paw button whenever the animal now is the SAME as the one that popped up just before (1-back), then in a second round taps back which burrows lit up.
interaction: Animals pop from a 2x2 (K-1) up to 3x3 (older) field of burrows, one at a time at a fixed pace. In MATCH mode the child taps one large paw button when the current animal repeats the one immediately before (1-back); above grade the rule shifts to 2-back (same as two-ago). Taps never advance the stream, so pace is fixed and only consistency is credited. In HIDEOUT mode a short run of burrows light in sequence and the child taps the lit burrows back from the array (picture/position recognition); re-tapping a chosen burrow de-selects it (revision). Level (n, or span length) rises after a clean run and falls after an error (1-up/1-down staircase).
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand watches two burrows show a fox then the same fox again and slaps the paw with a check (about 6s); one unscored warm-up 1-back run follows. The repeat-the-animal idea reads instantly with no words.

learning_science.why: Detecting a repeat n items back forces constant encode-compare-drop of the WM buffer, a classic updating index that scales from an easy 1-back for K-1 to a 2-back above grade.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 starts at 1-back with one large animal target at a fixed pace, and the staircase only raises n after high accuracy so pace never rewards speed.
learning_science.source: Kirchner 1958; Jaeggi et al. 2008

learning_science.why: Reproducing which locations lit indexes visuospatial short-term span, a capacity separable from verbal span.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The HIDEOUT recognition shell reuses the same burrows so no new instructions are needed, and span is staircased upward from 2.
learning_science.source: Corsi 1972; Kessels et al. 2000

learning_science.why: RT variability and lapses track ability better than fastest RT and are less coachable.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scoring credits sustained accuracy and low RT variability, not fast taps; telemetry surfaces CV and lapses and never a speed score.
learning_science.source: Larson & Alderton 1990

tail_precision_rationale: d-prime separates true 1-/2-back match detection from a liberal tapper; the updating cost from 1- to 2-back and the staircased visuospatial span give continuous capacity indices that keep separating high performers after simple-accuracy ceilings, while RT variability adds a coach-resistant consistency signal.
age_rationale: One large target and a single paw button need only a coarse tap, so K-1 motor demand is minimal; 1-back suits 5-6 year-olds while 2-back and larger grids extend the ceiling upward. The K-8 tag covers the grade-spanning picture-recognition item.

adaptive.content_range: 1-back to 3-back; visuospatial span 2-6; 2x2 to 3x3 field
adaptive.difficulty_levers: n level, span length, field size, pace
adaptive.notes: Animals and burrow layouts are freely swappable, giving unlimited matched parallel forms for cloned near-cut items.

engagement_hook: Whack-a-mole style peek-a-boo: animals pop up and the child gets to catch the copycat, which is intrinsically playful for young children.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor: single large button and big burrow targets avoid fine-motor load. Familiarity: a wordless demo plus warm-up equalizes video-game exposure. Reading: none; all cues are pictorial. Device: fixed pace is tuned to slow hardware and taps never need to be fast, only correct.

name: Echo Drums (play-it-back span + beat count + same-drum 1-back)
one_liner: Animal drums light and bong one at a time; the child plays the beat back in order (or reversed, or smallest-to-biggest), counts how many times a drum sounded, and can flag when a drum repeats the one just before.
interaction: A row of large animal drums glows and sounds in a sequence. In ECHO mode the child taps the drums back: forward (repeat), REVERSE (backward), or SORTED smallest-to-biggest by the animal's real-life size (list sorting); a numbers shell puts digits on the drums for a digit-span analog. In COUNT mode one drum bongs several times per turn and after a few turns the child taps back how many bongs each turn had, in order (counting span). In SAME mode the child taps a paw when this drum matches the one immediately before (1-back). Re-tapping a filled slot returns the item (revision); span/length adapts plus or minus one each trial.
self_teach: The ghost-hand watches three drums glow then taps them back in the same order with a check (about 7s); one unscored warm-up echo follows. Reverse and sort rules are shown by a wordless backward arrow or a small-to-big ramp icon.

learning_science.why: Reproducing an ordered sequence indexes short-term storage, and sorting by size adds a manipulation demand (storage plus reordering).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Forward, reverse, and size-sorted modes reuse the same drums so the added demand is the only change; digits on drums give a digit-span analog for grades 2-3+.
learning_science.source: NIH Toolbox List Sorting; Wechsler Digit Span

learning_science.why: The drop from forward storage to backward/reorder isolates central-executive manipulation, which tracks fluid reasoning better than raw storage.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Matched forward and reverse staircases let telemetry report the span difference as a manipulation-cost signal.
learning_science.source: Engle 2002; St Clair-Thompson & Gathercole 2006

learning_science.principle: Counting span as a complex-span processing+storage task
learning_science.why: Counting the bongs (processing) while holding earlier counts (storage) is the child counting-span paradigm.
learning_science.concrete_decision: COUNT mode gates the stored score on counting accuracy so a child cannot trade away counting to boost recall.
learning_science.source: Case, Kurland & Goldberg 1982

tail_precision_rationale: The staircased span threshold and the forward-minus-backward manipulation cost are continuous capacity/executive indices that avoid ceiling; the counting-span processing-accuracy gate protects comparability, and order-vs-item error tags refine near-cut placement beyond right/wrong.
age_rationale: Tapping large drums in order is within K-1 motor range and needs no reading (pictures/sounds); digit, reverse and sort modes and longer spans extend difficulty upward. The K-8 tag covers the grade-spanning forward/backward sequencing item.

adaptive.content_range: span 2-8; forward/reverse/sorted; picture or digit tokens; 1-3 counting turns
adaptive.difficulty_levers: span length, recall order (forward/back/sort), token type, count magnitude
adaptive.notes: Drum sets, animal identities, and digit strings are swappable for endless matched parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Making music by echoing a beat is inherently rewarding, and catch-the-drum-that-repeats adds a playful vigilance game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor: large drum and slot targets avoid fine-motor precision. Familiarity: wordless demo plus warm-up. Reading: none in picture mode; digit mode is opt-in for grades that know numerals. Device: audio is supportive not required (drums also glow) and pacing tolerates slow hardware.

name: Frog Lily-Count (child counting span)
one_liner: Frogs hop onto each lily pad and the child counts them by tapping each frog; a leaf then hides the pad, and after a few pads the child taps back how many frogs were on each pad, in order.
interaction: On each pad 1-5 frogs hop on among a few distractor bugs; the child taps each frog to count it (processing), then a leaf covers the pad and the count is committed. After N pads (set size) a pond of number-lily-pads appears and the child taps the counts back in pad order (storage); a SORT toggle instead asks for the counts smallest-to-largest (list sorting). Re-tapping a placed count returns it (revision). Set size rises after a correct recall with accurate counting and falls after an error (staircase).
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps the two frogs on a pad, the leaf closes, a second pad shows three frogs, then it taps 2 then 3 on the number pads with a check (about 8s); one unscored warm-up at set size 2 follows.

learning_science.why: Alternating an active count with storage of prior counts is the canonical child complex-span task, loading the central executive rather than only the phonological store.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractor bugs force genuine counting (not subitizing) and the stored recall is order-sensitive, matching the counting-span construct.
learning_science.source: Case, Kurland & Goldberg 1982

learning_science.why: Complex-span validity depends on the child actually doing the processing task instead of ignoring it to hoard recall.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A minimum counting accuracy is required for a recall to count toward the span estimate, surfaced as a processing-accuracy telemetry field.
learning_science.source: Conway et al. 2005; Unsworth & Engle 2007

learning_science.why: Ceiling/max load reached is the sharpest single tail statistic, so the task must extend above grade.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Set size escalates until the child fails, estimating a counting-span threshold rather than a fixed-length pass/fail.
learning_science.source: Larson & Alderton 1990

tail_precision_rationale: The staircased counting-span threshold is a continuous capacity index that keeps separating high performers, the processing-accuracy gate keeps the storage score comparable across children, and the accuracy-by-set-size slope (updating cost) turns one construct into a load curve for finer tail resolution.
age_rationale: Counting a few frogs and tapping number pads needs only coarse taps and small-number counting available to most kindergartners; larger counts and set sizes extend the ceiling for older children.

adaptive.content_range: count 1-5 per pad; set size 2-6; ordered or size-sorted recall
adaptive.difficulty_levers: count magnitude, set size, distractor density, recall order
adaptive.notes: Pad counts and creatures are procedurally generated for unlimited matched parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Cute frogs hopping onto pads make a counting chore feel like a pond game, sustaining young children's effort.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor: tapping frogs and pads is coarse. Familiarity: wordless demo plus warm-up. Reading: none; counts are shown as dot/number pads. Device: counting is untimed so slow hardware does not penalize; only counting accuracy and recall order are scored.

name: Bubble Count Catch (selective counting span + same-count 1-back)
one_liner: Each burst of bubbles has some target-color bubbles mixed with others; the child counts only the target bubbles, remembers each burst's count, and can also flag when a burst has the same target-count as the one before.
interaction: A burst of mixed-color bubbles floats up and the child taps only the target-color bubbles to count them (processing with selective attention). After N bursts the child taps back the target-counts in burst order (counting span). In SAME-COUNT mode the child instead taps a paw when the current burst holds the same number of target bubbles as the immediately preceding burst (a quantity 1-back); above grade this becomes same-as-two-bursts-ago (2-back). Set size or n adapts with performance and counting must stay accurate for the recall to count.
self_teach: The ghost-hand pops the two red bubbles in a burst (ignoring blue ones), a second burst shows three red, and it taps 2 then 3 on the count pads with a check (about 8s); one unscored warm-up follows.

learning_science.why: Counting a target color among distractors adds attentional filtering on top of counting-span storage, sharpening the executive load.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractor bubbles must be filtered so the processing step genuinely taxes attention rather than allowing subitizing.
learning_science.source: Case, Kurland & Goldberg 1982; Engle 2002

learning_science.why: Comparing the current count to n bursts back requires updating a magnitude buffer, a nonverbal updating index appropriate before fluent numerals.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The SAME-COUNT 1-back uses quantities (not symbols) so young children can play, with a 2-back above-grade extension.
learning_science.source: Kirchner 1958; Halford, Wilson & Phillips 1998

learning_science.why: Sustained accuracy and low variability index ability better than fast responses.
learning_science.concrete_decision: No speed bonus; the paw and count pads accept unhurried responses and telemetry reports variability and lapses, not raw RT.
learning_science.source: Larson & Alderton 1990

tail_precision_rationale: It yields both a counting-span threshold (with a processing-accuracy gate) and a magnitude-updating d-prime with false-alarm control, so a single game separates storage capacity from updating precision; the load/n staircase pinpoints each child's edge for sharp tail placement.
age_rationale: Popping a few bubbles and judging same-many relies on nonsymbolic quantity available in K-1; larger counts, more distractors, and 2-back extend difficulty upward.

adaptive.content_range: target count 1-6; distractor density; set size 2-6; 1-back or 2-back
adaptive.difficulty_levers: count magnitude, distractor ratio, set size, n level
adaptive.notes: Bubble colors, counts, and burst orders are generated for unlimited matched near-cut clones.

engagement_hook: Popping bubbles is a satisfying, low-stakes action that keeps the counting task feeling like play.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor: bubbles are large and mis-taps are logged, not penalized as capacity. Familiarity: wordless demo plus warm-up. Reading: none; quantities and counts are pictorial. Device: floats are slow and untimed for counting so frame-rate does not bias the score.

name: Rule-Flip Farm (DCCS sort with an opposite gate)
one_liner: The child sends bivalent animal cards into one of two barns by the rule shown on a flag - by colour, then the flag flips to sort by animal - and at an opposite gate must send the card the other way on purpose.
interaction: Each card shows an animal that has both a colour and a kind (e.g., a red rabbit). A flag banner sets the sorting rule (a paint-splat = sort by colour; an animal-silhouette = sort by kind) and the child taps the LEFT or RIGHT barn. In DCCS mode the rule holds for a run then switches (pre- and post-switch trials are logged for perseveration). In BORDER mode a per-card badge cues the rule trial-by-trial for rapid switching. At an OPPOSITE gate (day/night banner) the child must send the card to the wrong barn on purpose (do-the-opposite); an older ink-word shell asks the child to route by ink colour while ignoring a printed colour word. Accuracy, switch-vs-repeat RT and perseverative errors are logged and nothing rewards fast taps.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sorts a red rabbit into the red barn under a paint flag, the flag flips to an animal icon, and it re-sorts by kind with a check (about 8s); one unscored warm-up per rule precedes any scored switch.

learning_science.why: Sorting bivalent cards by one dimension then switching to the other is the standard early set-shifting measure, sensitive to preschool executive development.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Post-switch trials are separated from pre-switch so perseveration (applying the old rule) is measured directly.
learning_science.source: Zelazo 2006; Frye, Zelazo & Palfai 1995

learning_science.why: Deliberately sending a card the wrong way, or naming ink over word, requires suppressing a prepotent response, integrating inhibition with flexibility.
learning_science.concrete_decision: An opposite gate and an older ink-word shell add a Stroop-like conflict whose interference cost is logged separately.
learning_science.source: Gerstadt, Hong & Diamond 1994; Stroop 1935

learning_science.why: Shifting, inhibition, and updating are related but separable; one flexible game can probe shifting and inhibition with shared surface features.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Rule-switch trials index shifting while opposite/ink trials index inhibition, reported as distinct telemetry.
learning_science.source: Miyake et al. 2000

tail_precision_rationale: Perseverative-error rate and switch cost isolate set-shifting efficiency while the congruency/interference cost isolates inhibition; near-zero perseveration and small switch/interference costs held at high accuracy are sharp, hard-to-coach executive markers that a single accuracy score blurs.
age_rationale: Two big barns and a single tap suit K-1 motor skills and DCCS is validated from age 3; border-cued rapid switching and the ink-word shell raise difficulty for grades 4-5 and up. The K-8 tag reflects the grade-spanning DCCS item.

adaptive.content_range: 1-2 sorting dimensions; blocked or trial-cued switches; optional opposite/ink conflict
adaptive.difficulty_levers: switch frequency, number of dimensions, conflict presence, cue lead time
adaptive.notes: Animals, colours and cue schedules are swappable for endless matched forms; ink-word shell reserved for readers.

engagement_hook: Sending animals home to the right barn, then a mischievous do-the-opposite gate, keeps rule-switching feeling like a farm game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor: two large targets, coarse taps. Familiarity: wordless demo plus per-rule warm-up. Reading: none for colour/kind sorting; the ink-word conflict shell is reserved for grades that read and never scores K-1. Device: untimed responses; only within-child switch/interference costs are interpreted, cancelling device latency.

name: Mirror Mischief (do-the-opposite + copy/opposite switch)
one_liner: A puppet shows an action or picture and the child must do the OPPOSITE - hands up when it puts hands down, tap night for a sun - while a banner can flip the game between copy and opposite.
interaction: A friendly puppet displays a prompt (arms up/down, big/small, a sun or moon, happy/sad). In OPPOSITE mode the child taps the opposite response button; in COPY mode the child matches it. A wordless banner sets and can flip the mode, so trials are copy-repeat, opposite-repeat, or a switch between the two (cognitive flexibility). A day/night shell taps night for a sun and day for a moon; an older ink-word shell taps the button matching the ink colour, not the printed word. Congruent (copy) and incongruent (opposite/conflict) trials are logged; responses are untimed and only accuracy, interference and switch cost are scored.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sees the puppet raise its arms and taps the ARMS-DOWN button with a check, then sees a sun and taps NIGHT (about 7s); one unscored warm-up of each rule follows.

learning_science.why: Producing the opposite of a shown action integrates working memory for the rule with inhibition of the prepotent copy response, a validated integrated-EF paradigm for young children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Big paired opposite buttons and a puppet model make the rule obvious without words, keeping it playable at K-1.
learning_science.source: Diamond 2013; NEPSY-II executive tasks

learning_science.why: Saying night to a sun requires suppressing the automatic semantic response, a classic preschool inhibition measure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The day/night shell uses pictures only so no reading is needed, with the ink-word Stroop reserved for older readers.
learning_science.source: Gerstadt, Hong & Diamond 1994

learning_science.why: Flipping between copy and opposite requires reconfiguring the response mapping, a flexibility demand separable from inhibition.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Copy/opposite switches are interleaved so switch cost can be measured on top of the interference effect.
learning_science.source: Miyake et al. 2000; Zelazo 2006

tail_precision_rationale: The incongruent-minus-congruent interference cost isolates inhibition independent of baseline speed, and the copy/opposite switch cost adds a flexibility axis; small costs held at high accuracy, plus adaptive post-error slowing, are coach-resistant tail markers of executive control.
age_rationale: Imitating or opposing a puppet with two big buttons is within K-1 range and needs no reading; the ink-word conflict shell and faster switch schedules extend the ceiling for older readers. The K-8 tag reflects the grade-spanning opposites/Stroop items.

adaptive.content_range: copy vs opposite; day/night; optional ink-word for readers; blocked or switching
adaptive.difficulty_levers: switch frequency, conflict strength, response-set size, prompt pace
adaptive.notes: Puppet actions and picture pairs are swappable; ink-word shell reserved for readers.

engagement_hook: A playful puppet daring the child to do the opposite turns inhibition into a giggle-inducing game of tricks.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor: two large buttons. Familiarity: wordless demo plus warm-up of each rule. Reading: none for action/day-night; ink-word shell reserved for readers and never scores K-1. Device: only within-child interference and switch costs are used, cancelling absolute device latency.

name: Shape Buddy Match (match-to-sample DCCS)
one_liner: A target buddy is shown and the child picks which of two choices goes with it by the current matching rule - by colour, then the rule quietly switches to shape - matching to sample as the rule changes.
interaction: A central target card (e.g., a blue star) appears with two choice cards below (a blue circle and a red star). A wordless rule banner (colour swatch or shape outline) sets whether to match by colour or by shape and the child taps the matching choice. After a run the banner switches the rule (DCCS match-to-sample); a harder shell hides the banner so the child must infer the current rule from feedback and detect the silent switch. Switch-vs-repeat accuracy and RT and perseverative errors are logged; responses are untimed and consistency, not speed, is credited.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sees a blue star under a colour banner and taps the blue circle (matching colour) with a check, then the banner turns to a shape outline and it taps the red star (matching shape) (about 8s); one unscored warm-up per rule follows.

learning_science.why: Matching a sample to one of two options by a switching rule is a standard computerized set-shifting task that avoids sorting motor demands.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Two large choice cards and a pictorial rule banner make the current rule obvious, and the banner-hidden shell adds rule discovery for older children.
learning_science.source: Zelazo 2006; Berg 1948 (WCST lineage)

learning_science.why: Continuing to match by the old rule after a switch directly indexes failure to update the task set.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Post-switch trials are isolated and old-rule responses are tagged as perseverative errors in the telemetry.
learning_science.source: Zelazo 2006; Miyake et al. 2000

learning_science.why: How quickly a child detects and adapts to an unannounced rule change indexes learning rate, adding incremental tail validity.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The banner-hidden shell changes the rule after a run of successes and logs trials-to-recovery.
learning_science.source: Grigorenko & Sternberg 1998

tail_precision_rationale: Switch cost and perseverative-error rate isolate shifting efficiency while first-action latency indexes rule-reconfiguration time; low perseveration and small switch cost held at high accuracy, plus fast recovery after silent switches, finely separate flexible reasoners at the tail.
age_rationale: Tapping one of two large cards to match a sample is within K-1 motor and cognitive range (DCCS is validated from age 3); the banner-hidden rule-discovery shell and faster switch schedules extend difficulty for older children. The K-8 tag reflects the grade-spanning DCCS item.

adaptive.content_range: match by colour or shape (extensible to size/number); cued or hidden rule; blocked or rapid switching
adaptive.difficulty_levers: switch frequency, cue visibility, number of match dimensions, choice similarity
adaptive.notes: Shapes, colours and rule schedules are procedurally generated for unlimited matched near-cut clones.

engagement_hook: Helping a buddy find its match, then noticing the rule sneakily change, makes flexibility feel like a friendly puzzle.
